reading.title: The Library at Night
reading.passage: The university library used to close at nine in the evening. Last term, after a survey showed that most students studied late, the school extended the closing time to midnight. The change was small but popular. Quiet reading rooms on the third floor now stay open, and a free shuttle bus runs every half hour to take students back to their dorms. Librarians say the number of evening visitors has doubled. Some staff members were worried about the extra cost, yet the school found that most of it went to lighting, which was already on for the security system. The library has also started a late-night help desk, where two senior students answer questions about finding books and using the databases.

questions.q: Why did the school change the library's closing time?
options: A new security system was installed.
A survey showed students studied late.
The shuttle bus was not busy at night.

questions.explain: a free shuttle bus runs every half hour to take students back to their dorms 指「每半小时一班的接驳班车」，故选定期往返的车辆。

questions.q: What can we learn about the extra cost?
options: It was much higher than expected.
It was paid by the students.
Most of it was for lighting that was already on.
It forced the library to close earlier again.
questions.explain: 第二段说 most of it went to lighting, which was already on for the security system——照明本就因安保系统开着，因此新增成本有限。

reading.title: A Short Walk After Lunch
reading.passage: A team of researchers followed 200 office workers for six weeks. Half of them were asked to walk for fifteen minutes after lunch; the others sat or returned to their desks as usual. At the end of the study, the walking group reported better concentration in the afternoon and fewer feelings of sleepiness. Their work output did not change much, but they said the break made the rest of the day feel easier. The researchers were careful not to claim too much. The sample was small, and people who chose to join may already have been more active. Still, the result agrees with earlier studies suggesting that light movement after a meal helps the body handle sugar more steadily. A short walk, the authors conclude, is a low-cost habit worth trying.

questions.q: What were half of the workers asked to do?
options: Walk for fifteen minutes after lunch
questions.explain: 第一段：Half of them were asked to walk for fifteen minutes after lunch.

questions.q: Which of the following did NOT change much according to the study?
options: How the rest of the day felt
questions.explain: Their work output did not change much（工作产出变化不大），而注意力和困倦感都有改善。

questions.q: What is the researchers' attitude towards the result?
options: They are certain it applies to everyone.
They think the study was wasted.
questions.explain: 第二段 were careful not to claim too much、sample was small 表明作者态度谨慎（cautious）。

reading.title: Why Old Phones Slow Down
reading.passage: Many people notice that a phone feels slower after two or three years. The reason is not always the hardware. New apps are written for newer devices, so they ask for more memory and faster processors than an old phone can offer. At the same time, a battery that has been charged hundreds of times holds less power, and the system may lower its speed to protect it. Storage matters too: when a phone is nearly full, it has trouble moving files around, which makes everything take longer. The good news is that simple steps help. Removing unused apps, clearing large videos and restarting the phone once a week can bring back much of its old speed. Replacing the battery is often cheaper than buying a new phone.

questions.q: According to the passage, why do new apps slow an old phone?
options: They are written to need more memory and faster processors.
They stop the battery from charging.
They delete files from the storage.
questions.explain: 第一段：new apps … ask for more memory and faster processors than an old phone can offer.

questions.q: What does the passage suggest about the battery?
options: It works better after hundreds of charges.
It is the only reason a phone slows down.
The system may reduce speed to protect a weak battery.
questions.explain: the system may lower its speed to protect it（系统可能降速以保护老化电池）。

questions.q: What is the main idea of the last paragraph?
options: Old phones should be thrown away.
Simple actions can make an old phone faster.
Batteries are more expensive than phones.
questions.explain: 末段列举删除不用应用、清理大视频、每周重启、换电池等低成本做法，主旨是「简单操作能让旧手机变快」。

reading.title: A Town That Bans Plastic Bags
reading.passage: A small coastal town stopped giving out free plastic bags last spring. Shopkeepers were nervous at first, but the town handed out cheap cloth bags to every household before the rule began. Six months later, volunteers collected rubbish along the beach and found far fewer plastic bags than in the same month of the previous year. Fishermen said the change also helped their nets, which used to get caught on floating plastic. Not everyone is happy. A few shop owners say that paper bags cost more and that some customers still forget to bring their own bag. The town council has now started a scheme that lets people borrow a bag from one shop and return it to another. Early figures suggest that most borrowed bags do come back.

questions.q: What did the town do before the rule started?
options: It gave cheap cloth bags to households.
questions.explain: the town handed out cheap cloth bags to every household before the rule began.

questions.q: Why were fishermen pleased with the change?
options: Fewer plastic bags got caught in their nets.
questions.explain: Fishermen said the change also helped their nets, which used to get caught on floating plastic.

questions.q: What problem do some shop owners still mention?
options: Paper bags cost more than plastic ones.
The beach is dirtier than before.
questions.explain: A few shop owners say that paper bags cost more and that some customers still forget…

reading.title: Learning to Cook from Grandmother
reading.passage: When Li Mei went to university, she could not cook even an egg. In her first winter holiday, her grandmother taught her five simple dishes, writing each step down in a small notebook. Li Mei took the notebook back to campus and began cooking for her roommates on Sundays. What started as a way to save money became the thing her friends looked forward to most. She now posts short videos of the same five dishes, and thousands of students watch them. She says the videos are not about showing skill: many viewers live far from home and miss familiar food. The notebook, now stained with oil, stays on her desk. Her grandmother's handwriting is hard to read, but Li Mei says she would not replace it with a printed recipe for anything.

questions.q: What did Li Mei's grandmother do?
options: She wrote down the steps of five dishes.
She bought Li Mei a printed recipe.
questions.explain: her grandmother taught her five simple dishes, writing each step down in a small notebook.

questions.q: Why does Li Mei make the videos?
options: To help students who miss food from home
To prove that she cooks better now
questions.explain: many viewers live far from home and miss familiar food——她强调视频不是炫技，而是抚慰想家的学生。

questions.q: What does the stained notebook suggest?
options: It has been used many times.
questions.explain: now stained with oil（沾满油渍）说明被反复使用；且她说不愿换成打印菜谱，可见其珍贵。

reading.title: The First Day at Work
reading.passage: On her first day at a design company, Chen Yu was given no big task. Her manager simply asked her to sit with three different teams and write down anything she did not understand. By Friday she had filled two pages with questions. Some were small, such as where files were kept; others were about why a client had rejected a draft. At the end of the week, the manager read the list with her and said it was the most useful thing a new employee had produced in months. Teams often forget what is confusing to an outsider, she explained. Chen Yu later learned that several of her questions led to a clearer internal guide. Looking back, she is glad her first job was to notice, not to pretend she already knew.

questions.q: What was Chen Yu asked to do in her first week?
options: Write down things she did not understand
questions.explain: asked her to sit with three different teams and write down anything she did not understand.

questions.q: Why did the manager value the list of questions?
options: It showed what was confusing to an outsider.
It contained a new design idea.
It proved Chen Yu worked fast.
questions.explain: Teams often forget what is confusing to an outsider——老员工习以为常之处恰是新人的价值所在。

questions.q: What did several of her questions lead to?
questions.explain: several of her questions led to a clearer internal guide.

reading.title: When a City Removes Its Fences
reading.passage: For decades the riverfront of the city was separated from the neighbourhoods behind it by a high fence and a busy road. Last year the council removed both, replacing the road with a wide path lined with trees. The stated aim was modest: give residents a place to walk. What followed was less modest. Within a year, small cafés and bookshops opened along the path, and property values in the adjacent streets rose sharply. Critics had warned that such improvements merely push poorer residents out, and the early figures partly bear them out: rents near the path have climbed faster than anywhere else in the city. Supporters reply that the answer is not to abandon public space but to build affordable housing at the same time. The dispute is unlikely to be settled soon, yet both sides now agree on one point — that a river which people can actually reach changes how a city thinks about itself.

questions.q: What was the council's original purpose in removing the fence and road?
options: To give residents a place to walk
To reduce traffic in the whole city
questions.explain: The stated aim was modest: give residents a place to walk.（公开宣称的目标很朴素：给居民一处散步之地）其余为后续结果。

questions.q: What does "the early figures partly bear them out" most probably mean?
options: The figures completely disprove the critics.
The figures partly support the critics' warning.
The critics refused to look at the figures.
The figures were collected by the critics.
questions.explain: bear out 意为「证实、支持」；紧接着 rents near the path have climbed faster 说明租金上涨，部分印证了批评者关于挤走低收入居民的警告。

questions.q: What do both sides in the dispute agree on?
options: Affordable housing should be the only priority.
The project should never have been started.
Reaching the river changes how the city sees itself.
Rents will stop rising next year.
questions.explain: 末句 both sides now agree on one point — that a river which people can actually reach changes how a city thinks about itself.

questions.q: What is the author's tone in describing the outcome?
questions.explain: 作者并列陈述支持与批评双方、用 modest / less modest / unlikely to be settled 等克制措辞，属客观观察而非赞扬或反对。

reading.title: Grades, Rewritten
reading.passage: Universities have long treated the exam as a clean measure of what a student knows. That confidence is quietly eroding. When a large online course compared the marks of students who sat the same paper in a quiet hall with those who took it at home with a screen open, the difference was not large enough to settle the argument — but it was large enough to unsettle it. More troubling was what happened afterwards: students who had been told their results were provisional went on to outperform their peers in the following term, while those given a fixed grade did not. The researchers are careful to say that a label is not a destiny. Still, if a number handed out in December can alter how much effort someone makes in March, then the exam is measuring something more than knowledge. It is also, inadvertently, helping to produce it.

questions.q: What did the comparison of exam marks show?
options: The difference was too small to be measured.
The difference was not decisive but was disturbing.
Quiet halls produced clearly better marks.
questions.explain: not large enough to settle the argument — but it was large enough to unsettle it：不足以定论，却足以让人不安。

questions.q: What happened to students told their results were provisional?
options: They performed better in the following term.
They asked to retake the exam.
questions.explain: students who had been told their results were provisional went on to outperform their peers in the following term.

questions.q: What does the last sentence imply about exams?
options: Exam results can influence the very ability they claim to measure.
questions.explain: 末句 helping to produce it：分数不仅「测量」知识，还反过来「制造/影响」了被测量的东西（后续努力）。

questions.q: Which word best describes the researchers' position?
questions.explain: The researchers are careful to say that a label is not a destiny：措辞审慎，拒绝过度推论。

reading.title: The Price of Cleaner Air
reading.passage: Few policies are as easy to praise and as hard to price as air quality regulation. A factory ordered to fit cleaner equipment faces a bill it can count; the benefit — fewer hospital visits across a region — is spread thinly over thousands of households and years, and therefore rarely appears in anyone's accounts. Economists have tried to close this gap by putting a number on avoided illness, but such figures are routinely attacked as speculative. The objection is not unreasonable, yet it is applied asymmetrically: the cost of compliance is treated as hard fact, while the cost of doing nothing is treated as guesswork. Several long-term studies now suggest that the latter has been consistently underestimated. If so, the familiar complaint that regulation is too expensive may rest less on arithmetic than on which column of the ledger we are willing to look at.

questions.q: Why is the benefit of cleaner air hard to account for?
options: It is spread over many households and years.
questions.explain: the benefit … is spread thinly over thousands of households and years, and therefore rarely appears in anyone's accounts.

questions.q: What does "applied asymmetrically" refer to?
options: Costs and benefits are judged by different standards.
Both sides use the same data.
questions.explain: 合规成本被当作 hard fact，而不作为的代价被当作 guesswork——同一把尺子没有用在两边，即标准不对称。

questions.q: What do several long-term studies suggest?
options: The cost of compliance has been exaggerated.
The cost of inaction has been underestimated.
Air quality has no effect on health.
questions.explain: Several long-term studies now suggest that the latter has been consistently underestimated（后者＝不作为的代价，被低估）。

questions.q: What is the main point of the passage?
options: Claims that regulation is too costly may reflect accounting bias.
questions.explain: 末句点题：所谓「监管太贵」，更多取决于我们愿意看账本的哪一栏，即核算口径的偏差。

reading.title: The Myth of the Empty Mind
reading.passage: We tend to assume that doing nothing is the absence of thought. Brain-imaging studies have made that assumption increasingly difficult to hold. When participants are left alone in a quiet room with no task, a network associated with memory, planning and self-reference becomes more, not less, active. Far from idling, the mind rehearses recent conversations, simulates tomorrow's difficulties and quietly rearranges what it knows. This may explain why solutions so often arrive in the shower rather than at the desk. It also complicates a familiar complaint about modern work: that constant interruption is merely a loss of time. If uninterrupted stretches are when the brain consolidates and recombines, then a calendar packed with short meetings is not only inefficient; it removes the very condition under which understanding forms. Rest, on this account, is not the reward for thinking but part of the machinery of it.

questions.q: What have brain-imaging studies shown about a person left with no task?
options: A network linked to memory and planning becomes more active.
Only visual areas of the brain respond.
The brain cannot be measured reliably.
questions.explain: a network associated with memory, planning and self-reference becomes more, not less, active.

questions.q: Why does the author mention solutions arriving in the shower?
options: To show that people think better when relaxed
To argue that showers save time
To introduce a new imaging technique
questions.explain: 「远非空转」的大脑会排演、模拟、重组已知，故答案常在淋浴时冒出——用以说明放松时思维仍在运作。

questions.q: What does the author suggest about a calendar full of short meetings?
options: It is the most efficient way to work.
It removes the condition needed for understanding to form.
It has no effect on how people think.
questions.explain: it removes the very condition under which understanding forms（恰恰剥夺了理解得以形成的条件）。

questions.q: What does the last sentence mean?
options: Rest should be earned by hard work.
Rest is a component of thinking itself.
Thinking is impossible without a desk.
questions.explain: Rest … is not the reward for thinking but part of the machinery of it：休息不是思考之后的奖赏，而是思考机制本身的一环。

reading.title: What a Dictionary Leaves Out
reading.passage: A dictionary tells us what a word may mean; it is remarkably silent on what a word has been allowed to mean. Consider the vocabulary of work. For much of the last century, terms such as "career" and "profession" were reserved for occupations that required formal qualifications, while the activities that filled most people's days were described with humbler verbs. The distinction was presented as neutral, a matter of precision. Yet it quietly sorted lives into those that progressed and those that merely passed. Linguists point out that such boundaries rarely survive contact with evidence: the skills required in so-called unskilled work often take years to acquire. What is interesting is not that the labels were unfair — that is easily said — but that they were so durable. A category, once printed, acquires the quiet authority of something that was always there; challenging it requires not a better definition but a willingness to notice that a definition was made at all.

questions.q: According to the passage, how were "career" and "profession" once used?
options: Only for work needing formal qualifications
questions.explain: terms such as career and profession were reserved for occupations that required formal qualifications.

questions.q: What does the author find most interesting about such labels?
questions.explain: What is interesting is not that the labels were unfair — that is easily said — but that they were so durable（耐人寻味的是其持久性）。

questions.q: What does "a category, once printed, acquires the quiet authority of something that was always there" suggest?
options: Written labels come to seem natural and unquestionable.
Old words are more precise than new ones.
questions.explain: 一旦被印成条目，分类就获得了「仿佛向来如此」的隐蔽权威——即被自然化、不再被质疑。

questions.q: Which statement would the author most likely agree with?
options: Definitions are discovered rather than made.
Better dictionaries will solve the problem.
We should notice that definitions are human constructions.
questions.explain: 末句：challenging it requires … a willingness to notice that a definition was made at all（意识到定义是被造出来的）。

reading.title: The Tool That Changed the Task
reading.passage: When a new automation tool was introduced into a hospital's records department, managers expected it to reduce headcount. Eighteen months later, staff numbers were unchanged, but the work was unrecognisable. Clerks who had spent their days transcribing forms now spent them checking the tool's output, handling the cases it flagged as uncertain, and explaining decisions to patients. The tool had not removed the job; it had relocated its difficulty to the edges, where judgement was still required. Researchers who studied the change call this the "residual problem": automation reliably handles the routine middle and leaves behind precisely those cases that are hardest to codify. The consequence is counter-intuitive. Because the remaining work is less repetitive, it demands more experience, not less — and the people doing it need support and training that the original plan had not budgeted for. Efficiency, it turns out, is not the same as simplification.

questions.q: What did managers expect the automation tool to do?
questions.explain: managers expected it to reduce headcount（缩减人员编制）。

questions.q: What happened to the clerks' work after eighteen months?
options: It shifted to checking, judging and explaining.
It was moved to another department.
questions.explain: checking the tool's output, handling the cases it flagged as uncertain, and explaining decisions to patients.

questions.q: What does the "residual problem" refer to?
options: The high cost of the software
The difficult cases automation leaves behind
Staff refusing to use new tools
questions.explain: automation reliably handles the routine middle and leaves behind precisely those cases that are hardest to codify.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Automation can make the remaining work more demanding.
Clerks need fewer skills than before.
questions.explain: 末两句点题：剩余工作更不重复、更需要经验，Efficiency … is not the same as simplification（效率≠简化）。
